## Q1
Arrange these language families from specialization to generalization.

A. All regular languages<br>
B. All Turing-acceptable languages<br>
C. All Turing-decidable languages<br>
D. All context-free languages

## Q1 - Options
(A) A, B, C, D
(B) A, C, B, D
(C) A, D, C, B
(D) A, D, B, C

## Q1 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Chomsky Hierarchy, Grammars & CNF/GNF
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2026 (22 Jun, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q26

Every regular language is context-free; every context-free language is decidable; and every decidable language is Turing-acceptable (recursively enumerable). The inclusions therefore grow as A, D, C, B.

## Q3
Match List-I (Grammar types) with List-II (Production forms).

| List-I (Grammar) | List-II (All productions are of the form) |
|---|---|
| A. Regular Grammar | I. A → aX, where a ∈ T and X ∈ V\* |
| B. Unrestricted Grammar | II. A → xB, A → x or A → Bx, A → x where A, B ∈ V and x ∈ T\* |
| C. Chomsky Normal Form | III. x → y, where x ∈ (V ∪ T)+ and y ∈ (V ∪ T)\* |
| D. Greibach Normal Form | IV. A → BC or A → a, where A, B, C are in V and a is in T |

## Q3 - Options
(A) A-II, B-III, C-I, D-IV
(B) A-I, B-III, C-II, D-IV
(C) A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I
(D) A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III

## Q3 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Chomsky Hierarchy, Grammars & CNF/GNF
**Source:** UGC NET Jan 2026 (2 Jan, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q10

Each grammar type has a distinct restriction on the shape of its productions.

A-II — Regular grammar productions are right-linear (A → xB or A → x) or left-linear (A → Bx or A → x), with x a string of terminals, matching item II.

B-III — Unrestricted grammar places no shape restriction beyond x containing at least one variable, matching the most general form x → y in item III.

C-IV — Chomsky Normal Form restricts every production to exactly two variables (A → BC) or a single terminal (A → a), matching item IV.

D-I — Greibach Normal Form requires every production to start with exactly one terminal followed only by variables (A → aX), matching item I.

A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I is therefore the correct match.

## Q4
*Editorially repaired version of an ambiguous NTA item.* Which grammars are context-free but not regular?

| Grammar | Productions |
|---|---|
| A | S → Ab; aS → aA; A → a |
| B | S → Ab; A → Sa; A → a |
| C | S → AS; S → aA; A → a |
| D | S → Ab; S → aA; A → a |
| E | S → Sb; A → Aa; A → ε |

## Q4 - Options
(A) A and B only
(B) C and D only
(C) C only
(D) A, B, D, and E only

## Q4 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Chomsky Hierarchy, Grammars & CNF/GNF
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2025 (26 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q72

A context-free grammar must have one nonterminal on the left of every production. A is not context-free because it has `aS → aA`. B, D, and E are regular because their productions are consistently linear. C is context-free but not regular because `S → AS` has two nonterminals on its right side. Thus only C qualifies. The source's answer set was repaired to include that result explicitly.

(B) A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II
(C) A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III

## Q5 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Chomsky Hierarchy, Grammars & CNF/GNF
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2025 (26 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q77

Type 3 grammars use the regular production form V → VΣ or Σ. Type 2 allows a single variable on the left, V → (V ∪ Σ)\*. Type 1 uses noncontracting contextual productions λVβ → λ(V ∪ Σ)*β, and Type 0 has unrestricted productions over (V ∪ Σ)*. This gives A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III.

Arrange the following Language Classes in ascending order according to their expressive power, as defined by Chomsky hierarchy:<br>
A. Context-free languages<br>
B. Context-sensitive languages<br>
C. Regular languages<br>
D. Unrestricted Grammars

## Q9 - Options
(A) (C), (A), (B), (D)
(B) (C), (A), (D), (B)
(C) (A), (C), (B), (D)
(D) (A), (D), (B), (C)

## Q9 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Chomsky Hierarchy, Grammars & CNF/GNF
**Source:** UGC NET Aug 2024 (23 Aug, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q77

By expressive power the Chomsky hierarchy runs regular ⊂ context-free ⊂ context-sensitive ⊂ unrestricted, recognised respectively by finite automata, pushdown automata, linear bounded automata and Turing machines. Ascending order is therefore (C), (A), (B), (D) — option A.

## Q10
The maximum yield length of the following CNF CFG is

S → AB<br>
A → CD<br>
B → e<br>
C → a<br>
D → b

## Q10 - Options
(A) 8
(B) 7
(C) 4
(D) 5

## Q10 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Chomsky Hierarchy, Grammars & CNF/GNF
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q52

This grammar is in Chomsky Normal Form because every rule is either A → BC (two nonterminals) or A → a (one terminal): S → AB, A → CD, B → e, C → a, D → b.

Since every nonterminal has exactly one production, there is only one possible derivation:<br>
S ⇒ AB ⇒ CDB ⇒ aDB ⇒ abB ⇒ abe

The derived string "abe" has length n = 3. A standard theorem for CNF grammars states that any derivation of a string of length n takes exactly 2n − 1 production steps. Here 2(3) − 1 = 5, which matches the derivation above (S→AB, A→CD, C→a, D→b, B→e is 5 steps).

- **A. 8** — this is the total node count of the full parse tree (5 nonterminal nodes + 3 terminal leaves), not the derivation length.
- **B. 7** — this is the edge count of the parse tree, one less than the total node count.
- **C. 4** — does not correspond to either the string length or the standard 2n − 1 step count.
- **D. 5** — correct. It matches 2n − 1 with n = 3, the number of production steps needed to derive the unique string "abe".

## Q11
Which of the following is ε-free grammar?

## Q11 - Options
(A) Type-0
(B) Type-1
(C) Type-2
(D) Type-3

## Q11 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Chomsky Hierarchy, Grammars & CNF/GNF
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (15 Mar, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q30

Type-1 (context-sensitive) grammars are defined to be non-contracting, meaning every production's right-hand side must be at least as long as its left-hand side.

This monotonicity rule forbids ε-productions in general, with only a single narrow exception allowing S → ε when S never appears on the right-hand side of any other rule, purely so the language can include the empty string. This is why context-sensitive grammars are commonly called ε-free (noncontracting) grammars.

Type-0 (unrestricted), Type-2 (context-free), and Type-3 (regular) grammars all permit ε-productions freely without any such restriction, so Type-1 is the one grammar class defined around avoiding them.

## Q13
What is the safest order while simplifying Context Free Grammar?

## Q13 - Options
(A) Elimination of ε-productions, Unit productions and then Useless symbols & productions.
(B) Elimination of useless symbols & productions, ε-productions and then Unit productions.
(C) Elimination of Unit productions, ε-productions and then Useless symbols and productions.
(D) Elimination of ε-productions, Useless symbols and productions and then Unit productions.

## Q13 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Chomsky Hierarchy, Grammars & CNF/GNF
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (11 Mar, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q83

Removing productions in the wrong order can reintroduce the very problems already cleaned up, which is why compiler theory fixes a specific safe order.

Eliminating ε-productions first prevents new unit productions from appearing, then eliminating unit productions next prevents new useless symbols from being missed, and eliminating useless symbols last removes anything left disconnected by the previous two steps.

This gives the safest order as ε-productions, then unit productions, then useless symbols and productions.

## Q14
The reduced grammar equivalent to the grammar, whose production rules are given below, is<br>
S → AB \| CA<br>
B → BC \| AB<br>
A → a<br>
C → aB \| b

## Q14 - Options
(A) S → CA, A → a, C → b
(B) S → CA \| B, B → BC \| B, A → a, C → aB \| b
(C) S → CA \| B, B → BC, A → a, C → aB \| b
(D) S → AB \| AC, B → BC \| BA, A → a, C → aB \| b

## Q14 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Chomsky Hierarchy, Grammars & CNF/GNF
**Source:** UGC NET Oct 2022 (8 Oct, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q12

First remove non-generating symbols, those that can never derive a terminal string.

Every production for B is B → BC or B → AB, and both alternatives still contain B itself, so B can never bottom out in a terminal string. B is non-generating and must be removed, along with every production that mentions it.

Removing B eliminates S → AB and C → aB, leaving S → CA and C → b as the only survivors alongside A → a.

Checking reachability from S confirms every remaining symbol (A, C) and the terminals they produce are reachable, so no further symbols are removed.

The reduced grammar is S → CA, A → a, C → b.
